rationale: While Greene et al. (2025) note in their abstract that all 25 dominant de novo cases display a severe and complex seizure phenotype, text within the paper notes that clinical 'Seizure' was formally annotated in only 89% of RNU2-2 cases, falling short of the hypothesized >95% penetrance threshold. Furthermore, independent reviews and studies (Jackson et al. 2025, Schatz et al. 2026) highlight variable expressivity, tendency for seizures, and individuals presenting with neurodevelopmental delay/intellectual disability with no seizure phenotype or reduced penetrance. In the biallelic recessive cohorts (Leitão et al. 2026, Jackson et al. 2026), seizures are frequent but not universal (e.g. generalized tonic-clonic seizures documented in 38 of 60 evaluated individuals), confirming incomplete epilepsy penetrance; however, whether dominant penetrance is strictly >95% remains contradicted by the 89% phenotypic annotation rate and reports of no-seizure presentations.

evidence.text: Greene et al. state in their abstract that all 25 dominant de novo cases displayed a severe and complex seizure phenotype, but text analysis indicates clinical seizure was annotated in 89% of cases.

conflicts: Greene et al. report in their abstract that all 25 dominant cases displayed a severe seizure phenotype, but also note in the text that 'Seizure' was coded/annotated in 89% of cases, conflicting with the claim of >95% penetrance.
Schatz et al. (2026) report variable expressivity and individuals presenting with 'no seizure phenotype' in RNU2-2 disorders, contradicting complete or near-complete penetrance.

new_directions.question_text: What proportion of dominant versus recessive RNU2-2 patients remain seizure-free into late adolescence and adulthood in unselected neurodevelopmental cohorts?
new_directions.rationale: Ascertainment bias from cohorts recruited specifically for developmental and epileptic encephalopathy (DEE) may artificially elevate reported epilepsy penetrance compared to broad intellectual disability cohorts.

new_directions.question_text: Do specific secondary alleles or modifying variants (such as n.99A) account for reduced seizure penetrance in non-epileptic carriers of pathogenic RNU2-2 alleles?
new_directions.rationale: Leitão et al. highlighted specific variants modifying penetrance; determining molecular modifiers could explain why a subset of patients with pathogenic variants escape clinical epilepsy.
